newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks dealt major blow by Sammi crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks dealt major blow by Sammi crisis.

text.p: South Korea's troubled banking industry, already reeling from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co, was dealt a new blow as Sammi Steel Co sought court protection, industry analysts said on Wednesday.
Sammi's failure sparked fears of higher interest rates, tighter credit to vulnerable small and medium-sized companies and worse terms for overseas borrowing, they said.
"This is a big disaster for the banking sector already in a state of shock from the Hanbo scandal," said Mok Young-chung, a banking analyst at ING-Barings Securities.
"Banks will now be more careful than ever in giving out loans."
Sammi Steel Co sought protection from its creditors on Tuesday along with four other affiliates of Sammi Group, South Korea's 26th largest conglomerate.
In January, Hanbo Steel filed for receivership under debts of $5.8 billion in South Korea's biggest corporate collapse.
Hanbo's bankruptcy had made it more difficult for Sammi to obtain fresh loans.
"We had more difficulty negotiating for fresh loans with financial institutions after the Hanbo scandal broke," said one Sammi executive, who declined to be identified.
"Banks squeezed their credit lines following the collapse of Hanbo and made it hard for companies such as Sammi Steel to borrow money," said Mok.
Analysts warned of a domino effect of corporate bankruptcies.
Many of South Korea's leading business groups -- including Hanwha, Ssangyong and Daewoo -- are heavily indebted.

South Korea's banking system was shaken by the Hanbo failure, which exposed weak credit analysis and corrupt lending practices. Three top bankers are now on trial for bribery in a loans scandal linked to the collapse.
As a result of the scandal, South Korean banks are paying more for overseas loans.
"Local banks' overseas borrowing costs are likely to rise, which would then be passed on to local companies," said Yoon Yong-chul, a banking analyst at SBC Warburg.
Korea First Bank is Sammi Steel's biggest creditor, with 395.9 billion won ($448.6 million) of outstanding loans at the end of 1996.
Korea First is also the biggest lender to Hanbo Steel. Moody's Investors Service dropped its long-term rating last month.
"This is a deadly blow to Korea First," said Im Joon-hwan, a banking analyst at Schroder Securities. "Its rating could be further downgraded."
Yoon of SBC Warburg said he now predicted Korea First could post a loss of 200 to 300 billion won this year after a profit of 6.25 billion won last year.
Korea First had 1.87 trillion won in non-performing loans with overdue interest of more than six months at the end of 1996, he said.
Sammi Steel had liabilities of 1.45 trillion won at the end of 1996 against assets of 1.53 trillion won, according to company figures.
Yields on benchmark three-year corporate bonds hit a new 18-month high of 12.85 percent on Wednesday, up from 12.75 percent on Tuesday. ($1 = 882.6 won)
